title: Problem Overview: Distance Frequency Gaps
content: Given **n points** in the plane with distinct distances d_1, ..., d_k ordered by frequency f(d_1) >= f(d_2) >= ..., Erdos asked: how large can the **frequency gap** f(d_1) - f(d_2) be? Clemen, Dumitrescu, and Liu (2025) proved the gap can be at least **Omega(n log n)** and conjectured a stronger bound of n^{1 + c / log log n}.
mathContext: This problem sits at the intersection of **combinatorial geometry** and **extremal combinatorics**. The frequency of a distance d is the number of unordered pairs of points at distance d. The Erdos distinct distances problem (resolved by Guth-Katz) controls how many distinct distances exist; this problem instead asks about the **distribution** of those distances -- specifically, how unevenly frequencies can be distributed among the top two distances.

title: Distance Frequency
content: **distFrequency A d** counts the number of unordered pairs {p, q} in A with dist(p, q) = d. Implemented by filtering the Cartesian product A x A for pairs at distance d (with p != q), then dividing by 2 to account for ordering.
mathContext: The division by 2 converts from ordered pairs to unordered pairs. For n points, the sum of all frequencies equals n choose 2 = n(n-1)/2, the total number of point pairs. This counting identity is formalized in the **total_pairs** theorem.

title: Distinct Distances
content: **distinctDistances A** computes the set of positive real distances realized by the point set A, by imaging the distance function over A x A and filtering out zero.
mathContext: See annotation content for formal details of distinct distances

title: Frequency Gap
content: **frequencyGap A** = maxFrequency A - secondFrequency A, measuring the drop from the **most frequent** distance to the **second most frequent**. A large gap means one distance dominates the configuration.
mathContext: The gap quantifies concentration: if one distance appears much more often than any other, the point set has a strong geometric bias toward that distance. For example, in a near-regular grid, the unit distance dominates, creating a large gap.

title: Main Conjecture (Omega(n log n) Gap)
content: **ErdosProblem959**: There exists C > 0 such that for all n >= 2, some n-point planar set has frequency gap at least **C * n * log n**. This asserts the gap grows superlinearly in n.
mathContext: The n log n threshold is natural: by the Erdos-Szekeres distinct distances bound (now Guth-Katz), n points have Omega(n / log n) distinct distances. Since frequencies sum to n(n-1)/2, a pigeonhole argument gives average frequency O(n log n). The conjecture says the **maximum** frequency can exceed the runner-up by this average amount.

title: Clemen-Dumitrescu-Liu Lower Bound (2025)
content: For every n >= 2, there exists an n-point planar set whose frequency gap is **Omega(n log n)**. This resolves the main conjecture affirmatively, taken as an axiom since the proof relies on intricate constructions from the 2025 paper.
mathContext: The construction builds point sets where one distance (typically the unit distance) appears n * log n times more than the second most frequent. The proof uses ideas from **additive combinatorics** and careful lattice-point constructions. The authors also establish generalized bounds for the r-th gap.

title: Stronger Conjecture (Superpolynomial Gap)
content: **ErdosProblem959_strong**: The frequency gap grows as n^{1 + c / log log n} for some c > 0. This is **superpolynomial** in n -- stronger than n log n but weaker than n^{1+epsilon} for any fixed epsilon.
mathContext: The exponent 1 + c / log log n tends to 1 from above, giving a growth rate between polynomial and truly superpolynomial. This matches the behavior seen in the **Erdos unit distance problem**, where the conjectured maximum count of unit distances is n^{1 + c / log log n}. The parallel suggests deep structural connections between frequency gaps and unit distance counts.

title: Generalized r-th Frequency Gap
content: **frequencyGapR A r** computes f(d_r) - f(d_{r+1}), the gap between the r-th and (r+1)-th most frequent distances. Frequencies are sorted in decreasing order and indexed; returns 0 if r is out of range.
mathContext: The generalized gap captures the full **frequency spectrum** of the distance set. The CDL generalized bound shows this gap is Omega(n log n / r) for 1 <= r <= log n, meaning the top O(log n) frequencies form a smoothly decreasing sequence rather than a single spike.

title: Total Pair Count Bound
content: The sum of all distance frequencies is at most **n choose 2** = n(n-1)/2. Each unordered pair contributes exactly one distance, so the total frequency count equals the number of pairs.
mathContext: This is the fundamental counting identity that connects distance frequencies to the size of the point set. Combined with the number of distinct distances, it yields average frequency bounds that motivate the Omega(n log n) conjecture.

title: Empty Set Base Case
content: **frequencyGap of the empty set is 0**, proved by unfolding definitions and simplifying the empty product. This serves as a base case for structural reasoning about the frequency gap.
